title: Boss: the bowling league scorer
summary: Test-drive bowling scores for a league app, pin a scorer you did not write against bonus bugs, and add running frame totals test-first.

steps.title: Ticket LEAGUE-19: score the games
body: The bowling league app records every roll and must show the score. The rules, from the league's handbook:
- A game is **10 frames**. In each frame the bowler has up to two rolls to knock down 10 pins.
- **Open frame**: fewer than 10 pins in two rolls; the frame scores the pins.
- **Spare**: all 10 in two rolls; the frame scores 10 plus the **next one** roll.
- **Strike**: all 10 with the first roll; the frame is over and scores 10 plus the **next two** rolls.
- In the 10th frame a spare earns one extra roll and a strike two, so the bonus can be counted. A perfect game (12 strikes) is 300.
Make a test list before typing any code. The bugs in bowling scorers hide in the bonuses and in the 10th frame.

steps.title: Test-drive the game
prompt: Test-drive `public class BowlingGame` with `public void Roll(int pins)` and `public int Score()`. `Roll` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for fewer than 0 or more than 10 pins. Assume the rolls are otherwise a valid, complete game when `Score()` is called.

Write `public class BowlingGameTests` as you go, at least **6** tests: gutter game, all ones, one spare, one strike, the perfect game, a spare in the 10th frame. The league's acceptance tests (`BowlingAcceptance`) run with yours.
starter: public void Roll(int pins) => throw new NotImplementedException();
public int Score() => throw new NotImplementedException();
void RollMany(int times, int pins) { for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) game.Roll(pins); }
solution: else if (rolls[i] + rolls[i + 1] == 10) { score += 10 + rolls[i + 2]; i += 2; }
void RollMany(int times, int pins) { for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) game.Roll(pins); }
template: [Fact] public void Gutter() => Assert.Equal(0, Play(new int[20]));
[Fact] public void Strike_then_spare() => Assert.Equal(40, Play([10, 5, 5, 5, 0, .. new int[14]]));
public void Impossible_rolls(int pins) => Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => new BowlingGame().Roll(pins));
hints: Store the rolls; compute the score in `Score()` by walking frame by frame with an index into the rolls.
A strike moves the index by one roll, any other frame by two. That is why the 10th frame's extra rolls are never counted as frames of their own.
Strike: `10 + rolls[i + 1] + rolls[i + 2]`; spare: `10 + rolls[i + 2]`; open: `rolls[i] + rolls[i + 1]`.
steps.explain: Counting by frames, not by rolls, is the design insight of this kata; tests for the spare, the strike and the 10th frame force it one step at a time.

steps.title: Pin a scorer you did not write
prompt: The mobile team wrote their own scorer. Before the app ships, you write the tests. It is compiled beside your tests:
else if (rolls[i] + rolls[i + 1] == 10) { score += 10 + rolls[i + 2]; i += 2; }
Write `public class BowlingScoreTests` with at least **5** tests (a `[Theory]` with `TheoryData<int[], int>` works well). Four planted bugs, all in the bonuses and the frame count.
starter: public void Gutter_game() => Assert.Equal(0, Bowling.Score(new int[20]));
solution: public static TheoryData<int[], int> Games => new()
public void Scores(int[] rolls, int expected) => Assert.Equal(expected, Bowling.Score(rolls));

hints: One game per rule: open frames (all ones), a single spare, a single strike, the perfect game.
A spare followed by a 3 is 16 in total; a strike followed by 3 and 4 is 24.
`[10, 3, 4, .. new int[16]]` builds a strike, two rolls and sixteen gutters.
steps.explain: Five games catch every bonus bug because each one isolates a single rule. The all-ones game alone catches the frame count bug: 18 instead of 20.

steps.title: Running totals for the scoreboard, test-first
prompt: The scoreboard shows the running total under each frame (see the handbook example: 20, 39, 48, ...). Test-drive `public static class Frames` with `public static IReadOnlyList<int> RunningTotals(IReadOnlyList<int> rolls)` for a complete game: ten numbers, the last one the final score.
Write your own `public class FramesTests` first, at least **3** tests. The acceptance tests (`FramesAcceptance`) include the handbook game.
starter: public static IReadOnlyList<int> RunningTotals(IReadOnlyList<int> rolls) => throw new NotImplementedException();
solution: else if (rolls[i] + rolls[i + 1] == 10) { score += 10 + rolls[i + 2]; i += 2; }
public void A_spare_waits_for_its_bonus() => Assert.Equal(new[] { 13, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16 }, Frames.RunningTotals([5, 5, 3, .. new int[17]]));
template: public void Gutter_game() => Assert.Equal(new int[10], Frames.RunningTotals(new int[20]));
public void Ten_totals_for_a_tenth_frame_spare() => Assert.Equal(10, Frames.RunningTotals([.. new int[18], 5, 5, 5]).Count);
hints: Start from the frame loop of the scorer and record the score after each frame.
The bonus rolls of the 10th frame belong to the 10th frame: the loop still runs exactly 10 times.
`Assert.Equal(new[] { 2, 4, 6, ... }, totals)` compares the whole list and shows the first position that differs.
steps.explain: The feature was a one-line change to a design that the earlier tests had already shaped: record the total inside the frame loop.
